"Sarita Bua, why is the old fort wall broken on one side?" Ritu asked as they walked past it to the market.
"Ah. There's a story. Three hundred years ago, the queen here refused to hand over the town to an invading army."
"Did she fight?"
"She did. The wall broke where the cannons hit. But she held the fort for forty days."
"Forty days! Then what?"
"They made peace. She kept the town, but paid a tax."
Ritu looked at the wall again. "So she didn't win or lose?"
"She protected her people. That's what the town remembers."
Ritu touched the broken stones. "I'm going to write about her for my project."

qa.a: Forty days.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she touched the broken stones?
qa.a: Ritu felt moved and proud, connecting the wall to the queen's story.

qa.q: How could Sarita Bua help Ritu learn more for her project?
qa.a: She could take Ritu to a local library or museum, or to an elder who knows more about the town's past.

qa.q: How does Sarita Bua see the queen's story?
qa.a: Sarita Bua sees it as a story about protecting people, not about winning or losing.

grounding: A child learns a piece of her town's history from her aunt.

When I was in Class 5, I thought history was just dates. Then my friend Akash's grandfather took us to the old church near our village in Goa.
He showed us a stone with carved ships. "This is where the fishermen prayed before the big storm of 1890," he said. "They all went out together, and they all came back, because they tied their boats to each other."
Akash and I stared at the ships. That night I kept thinking about the tied boats.
Our teacher later read us a Panchatantra story about doves caught in a net who flew away together. The same idea.
I'm Francis. I still think of that stone when I work in a group.

qa.q: What was carved on the stone?
qa.a: Ships.

qa.q: What was Francis feeling that night, thinking about the tied boats?
qa.a: Francis felt fascinated and moved by how the fishermen survived together.

qa.q: What could Francis do to learn more local stories?
qa.a: Francis could ask other elders in the village about old events and visit other places like the church.

qa.q: How might Akash's grandfather feel sharing this story?
qa.a: He likely feels proud and happy to pass the village's history to the children.

grounding: A young person recalls learning a local story whose moral matched a folk tale.

Tonight Kalyani paati lit the lamp and sat quietly, like she does every evening. Usually I watch TV. Today the power was off, so I sat with her.

qa.a: Find actual studies or data to support his claim, and prepare answers to likely counter-arguments.

qa.q: How does Thomas see Manoj's first argument?
qa.a: Thomas thinks it's just a claim based on one person's opinion, not solid evidence.

grounding: Two teens practise building claims with evidence and answering counter-arguments.

So there was this ad for a toothpaste, right? Big letters: "9 out of 10 dentists recommend." I told my friend Sahil, that's it, I'm switching.
Sahil's like, "Which ten dentists? Did they ask a thousand and pick ten?" I laughed at first. Then I thought about it.

qa.q: What did the toothpaste ad say in big letters?
qa.a: "9 out of 10 dentists recommend."

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling on first seeing the ad?
qa.a: Abhinav felt convinced and ready to switch, trusting the big number.

qa.q: What question could anyone ask when an ad uses numbers?
qa.a: Ask "out of how many?" and "compared to what?", and read the small print.

qa.q: How does Sahil see numbers in ads?
qa.a: Sahil is sceptical and wants to know how the numbers were chosen before believing them.

grounding: A teen tells how a friend's question taught Abhinav to doubt statistics in an ad.

passage:
I'm Mehak. In our Class 9 maths class, the teacher showed a news headline: "Cases of the flu doubled this month!"
Darshan, who sits next to me, frowned and wrote something. Then he put up his hand.
"Doubled from what? If it was two cases and now it's four, that's not scary."
The teacher smiled and showed the real numbers. It went from a small number to a slightly bigger one.
Darshan looked satisfied, not smug. He just wrote "percent vs actual" in his notebook.
I don't know if he was worried or just curious. But now I ask the same thing about every headline.

qa.q: What did Darshan write in his notebook?
qa.a: "percent vs actual".

qa.q: What might Darshan have been feeling when he frowned at the headline?
qa.a: Darshan was probably curious and doubtful, sensing the headline might be misleading.

qa.q: What habit could students take from Darshan's question?
qa.a: Always ask what the starting number was before being alarmed by "doubled" or big percentages.

qa.q: How does Mehak see Darshan's question?
qa.a: Mehak isn't sure of Darshan's feelings but finds the question useful and starts asking it too.

grounding: A classmate watches a teen question a misleading statistic in a headline.

passage:
Before: In June, Varun was sure he had a lucky streak. His cricket team had won the toss five times in a row. "I'll call heads again. Heads always wins," he told Gautam.
During: In maths class a week later, the teacher had everyone toss a coin a hundred times. Varun got heads five times in a row, then tails six times. His total was close to fifty-fifty.
"Each toss doesn't remember the last," the teacher said.
After: At the next match, Varun called tails. They lost the toss. Gautam teased him. Varun shrugged. "It's still fifty-fifty. I'm not special."
He sounded almost relieved.

qa.q: How many times had Varun's team won the toss in a row?
qa.a: Five times.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he said "I'm not special"?
qa.a: Varun felt calm and almost relieved, no longer believing he had to keep a lucky streak.

qa.q: What did the coin experiment teach Varun?
qa.a: That each toss is independent and streaks happen by chance, so there is no lucky side.

qa.q: How might Gautam see Varun's shrug?
qa.a: Gautam may be surprised that Varun doesn't care about losing the toss anymore.

grounding: Over weeks a teen learns that streaks happen by chance and each coin toss is independent.

passage:
The ad on the Mumbai bus stop said: "Students who drink BrainBoost score higher!" There was a smiling topper with a trophy.
Madhav nudged Farida. "Maybe I should drink it before my exam."
Farida squinted. "Who says they score higher? The company?"
"Probably."
"And maybe kids who drink it have parents who can afford tuition too. So is it the drink or the tuition?"
Madhav thought. "So they go together, but the drink might not cause it."
"Exactly. Correlation isn't causation. Sir said so in science."
Madhav looked at the smiling topper again. "Still, the trophy looks nice."
Farida laughed. "Study for the trophy, not the drink."

qa.q: What did the bus stop ad say?
qa.a: "Students who drink BrainBoost score higher!"

qa.q: What was Madhav feeling when he thought about drinking it before his exam?
qa.a: Madhav felt hopeful and a bit tempted by the promise.

qa.q: What question did Farida ask that helped Madhav think better?
qa.a: She asked whether something else, like tuition, could explain the scores instead of the drink.

qa.q: How does Farida see the advert's claim?
qa.a: Farida is doubtful because the company made the claim and it confuses things that go together with causes.

grounding: A teen explains to a friend why a drink ad confuses correlation with causation.

"Did you see this forward?" said Hansa, holding out her phone. "Kids who eat breakfast get better marks. So I'm eating breakfast before every test."
Neelam read it. "It says 'studies show'. Which studies?"
"It doesn't say."
"And maybe kids who eat breakfast also sleep on time and have calmer mornings. That could be the real reason."
"So breakfast doesn't help?"
"It might. But the forward doesn't prove it. And it's from someone called 'Health Tips 4U'."
Hansa laughed. "Okay, that's not a scientist."
"Eat breakfast because it's good for you anyway. Just don't trust a forward because it's shared a hundred times."

qa.q: What was the forward from?
qa.a: Someone called 'Health Tips 4U'.

qa.q: What was Hansa feeling when she laughed?
qa.a: Hansa felt amused and a little embarrassed at believing the forward so quickly.

qa.q: What could Hansa do next time a forward says "studies show"?
qa.a: She could check which studies, who wrote it, and whether something else could explain the link.

qa.q: How does Neelam see forwards shared many times?
qa.a: Neelam thinks being shared a lot doesn't make something true.

grounding: Two teens question a forwarded message's claim about breakfast and marks.

passage:
In Class 8, I believed my blue pen was lucky. Every time I used it, I got good marks. I was sure the pen caused it.
My friend Hrithik laughed at me. "Did you also study more on those days?"
I got annoyed. "It's the pen."
So Hrithik said, "Test it. Next test, study the same but use a different pen."
I did. I used a black pen, and studied just as hard. I got the same marks.
I felt a bit silly. Now, when someone says "this caused that," I think of my blue pen. I'm Dhruv, and I still have it, but only because it writes smoothly.

qa.q: What colour was the pen Dhruv thought was lucky?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when getting annoyed at Hrithik?
qa.a: Dhruv felt defensive and irritated about the lucky pen being questioned.

qa.q: What did Hrithik suggest that turned Dhruv's belief into a test?
qa.a: Hrithik suggested changing only the pen while studying the same, which showed the pen didn't cause the marks.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel when Dhruv gets the same marks?
qa.a: Hrithik is likely amused and pleased that the test proved the point.

grounding: A young person recalls testing a belief that a lucky pen caused good marks.
